newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-NICKLAUS JUST LOVES TO HAVE FUN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-NICKLAUS JUST LOVES TO HAVE FUN.

text.p: Jack Nicklaus knows how unlikely he is to win the British Open at Royal Troon this week but he would love to have as much fun as he did last year -- and for a little longer.

A year ago at Royal Lytham, the venerable American defied a bad back that threatened his participation to stand joint second just one shot off the lead after his best first 36 holes -- 69-66 -- in 35 successive trips to the tournament.
Then he went to pieces as he soared to a third-round 77 and a closing 73 left him mired down in joint 45th place.
"It was fun for the first half, then not too good after that. But it's been a while since I had such fun," he said at the time.
This year, in his 36th visit, the 57-year-old American who is regarded as the finest player the game has ever had has no illusions about his prospects.

"I feel like I'm hitting the ball decently so that's good for me. I don't think you're going to find me on Sunday evening coming down the 18th fairway at seven o'clock but I'd like to come down sometime in the afternoon."
Nicklaus, who won the title in 1966, 1970 and 1978, said a year ago that 1996 might be his last appearance at the Open until the Millennium Open at St Andrews in 2000.
But his recent form was sufficiently encouraging to attract him back.
The winner of a record 20 major titles was joint eighth in the senior players' championship in Detroit last week after being right in contention halfway.
He decided after his first two rounds of 69-67 to come here, "then as soon as I made the decision, I didn't play very well.
"My decision on coming here has always been made on how I'm playing and how I think I can play and whether I think I can handle the weather body-wise," he said.
"The first two rounds in Detroit I played very well and felt good. I said 'Well if I feel like I can be competitive then I'd kick myself in the rear end if I didn't go.'

He knows that the title is really up for grabs among the top five players who are playing well -- Tiger Woods, Ernie Els, Greg Norman, Colin Montgomerie and titleholder Tom Lehman, all of whom have won tournaments in recent weeks.
Everyone seems to have put those five on their shortlist -- along with 1994 champion Nick Price of Zimbabwe. Those six hold the top six places in the world rankings.
The weather will be a vital factor. It will be dry with winds blowing through the morning and increasing to 40 kph in the afternoon.
That could lead to a clutch of high scores, with players seeking to make their scores on the downwind front nine before tying to survive over a demanding back nine with the wind in their faces.
